name: Right ventricle
func: The lower right chamber of the heart. It pumps oxygen-poor blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and on to the lungs, where the blood picks up oxygen and drops off carbon dioxide.

levels.kid:
The **right ventricle** is the bottom room on the right side of your heart.

Blood that has already given its oxygen to your body comes into this room. Then the right ventricle **squeezes** and sends the blood on a short trip to your **lungs**.

In your lungs, the blood drops off the old air your body doesn't need and picks up fresh **oxygen** from the air you breathe in. Then it goes back to the heart to be sent all over your body.

Because the lungs are so close, the right ventricle doesn't have to push very hard. So its wall is thinner than the left side's.
levels.hs:
The **right ventricle** is the lower right chamber of the heart. It is the **most anterior** chamber, lying right behind the **sternum**, and it forms most of the front surface of the heart and part of its lower surface resting on the **diaphragm**. It sits to the right of and in front of the **left ventricle**, with the **interventricular septum** between them. Above it is the **right atrium**, connected through the **tricuspid valve**.

When the ventricle contracts, the tricuspid valve snaps shut and blood is pushed up through the **pulmonary valve** into the **pulmonary trunk**, which splits into the right and left **pulmonary arteries** to the lungs.

In cross-section the right ventricle looks like a **crescent** wrapped around the round left ventricle. Its wall is only about **3–5 mm** thick, much thinner than the left ventricle's, because the lungs are a **low-pressure** system. Normal right ventricle pressure peaks at around 25 mmHg, compared with about 120 mmHg in the left.

Inside, cord-like **chordae tendineae** attach the tricuspid valve flaps to **papillary muscles**, which pull tight during contraction so the valve does not flip backward into the atrium.
levels.college:
The right ventricle has three parts: an **inlet** (the tricuspid valve and its supporting apparatus), a heavily **trabeculated apex**, and a smooth-walled **outlet** called the **infundibulum** (conus arteriosus), leading to the pulmonary valve. The inflow and outflow are separated by a muscular arch, the **supraventricular crest**.

**Internal features**:
- **Trabeculae carneae**: irregular muscular ridges lining the walls.
- **Papillary muscles**: usually **anterior** (the largest), **posterior** and **septal**, connected by **chordae tendineae** to the three tricuspid leaflets (anterior, posterior and septal).
- **Septomarginal trabecula** (moderator band): a muscular bridge from the septum to the base of the anterior papillary muscle, carrying the **right bundle branch**, so that the anterior papillary muscle contracts on time.

**Valves**: the **tricuspid valve** has the largest opening of the four valves. The **pulmonary valve** has three semilunar cusps; unlike the aortic sinuses, the pulmonary sinuses give off no coronary arteries.

**Blood supply** comes mainly from the **RCA** (acute marginal branches and the posterior descending artery in right-dominant hearts), with the **LAD** supplying the anterior septum and a strip of the anterior right ventricle. Because the RV is perfused during both systole and diastole (its wall pressure is low), it tolerates ischemia relatively well.

**Contraction** is mainly longitudinal, shortening from base to apex, plus inward movement of the free wall and help from the septum (**ventricular interdependence**). Measurements like **TAPSE** on echo track this longitudinal motion.
levels.phd:
The right ventricle is a **volume pump** tuned to a low-resistance, highly compliant pulmonary circuit. Pulmonary vascular resistance is roughly one-tenth of systemic resistance, so the RV produces the same cardiac output with about one-sixth of the left ventricle's work. Its pressure–volume loop is more triangular, with ejection continuing even as pressure falls.

The RV is extremely sensitive to **afterload**. A sudden rise in pulmonary pressure (as in massive pulmonary embolism) causes rapid dilation and failure because the thin wall cannot generate much pressure. Gradual rises (as in chronic pulmonary hypertension) trigger **adaptive hypertrophy**; the key prognostic concept is **RV–pulmonary arterial coupling**, the ratio of ventricular contractility (end-systolic elastance) to arterial load (arterial elastance). Failure ensues when coupling breaks down.

During RV maladaptation, cardiomyocytes shift metabolism from fatty acid oxidation to **glycolysis**, show capillary rarefaction, fibrosis and mitochondrial changes; research targets include these metabolic pathways.

**Ventricular interdependence** occurs because the ventricles share a septum and pericardium. In RV pressure overload, the septum flattens and bows toward the LV (a "**D-shaped**" left ventricle on echo), reducing LV filling and output, so RV failure lowers systemic blood pressure.

Developmentally, the RV and outflow tract derive largely from the **second heart field** (ISL1, HAND2), while the LV comes from the first heart field. HAND2-deficient mice lack a right ventricle. Abnormal **outflow tract** septation and rotation underlie **tetralogy of Fallot** and transposition. The RV is also the main site of **arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy**, caused by mutations in **desmosomal** proteins (PKP2, DSP), in which muscle is replaced by fibrofatty tissue.
levels.expert:
**Exam signs of RV strain or failure**: a raised **JVP**, a **left parasternal heave** (an enlarged RV lifting the chest wall), a loud pulmonary component of S2, peripheral edema, an enlarged liver and ascites. Tricuspid regurgitation murmurs increase with inspiration (**Carvallo sign**).

**Acute RV failure**: **massive pulmonary embolism** causes RV dilation, low blood pressure and raised troponin and BNP. ECG may show sinus tachycardia, right axis deviation, right bundle branch block or the **S1Q3T3** pattern. **CT pulmonary angiography** confirms it; echo shows RV dilation and the **McConnell sign** (RV free wall hypokinesis with a preserved apex). Treatment includes anticoagulation and, for high-risk cases, clot-dissolving therapy or catheter or surgical removal.

**RV infarction** accompanies about a third of **inferior MIs** (proximal RCA occlusion): low blood pressure, raised JVP and clear lungs. ST elevation in right-sided lead **V4R** confirms it. These patients depend on filling pressure, so medicines that lower preload, such as nitrates, can cause dangerous drops in blood pressure.

**Cor pulmonale**: RV failure caused by lung disease or pulmonary hypertension. **Tetralogy of Fallot** includes RV outflow obstruction, VSD, an overriding aorta and **RV hypertrophy** (boot-shaped heart on X-ray). Repaired patients often develop pulmonary regurgitation and need valve replacement later.

**Arrhythmogenic RV cardiomyopathy** causes ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death in young athletes; cardiac MRI and epsilon waves on the ECG support diagnosis.

**Pacemaker and defibrillator leads** usually sit in the RV apex or septum. On imaging, **RV-to-LV diameter ratio** above about 1.0 on CT suggests RV strain.

keyPoints: Most anterior chamber, behind the sternum; crescent-shaped around the left ventricle
Pumps blood through the pulmonary valve to the lungs at low pressure (about 25 mmHg)
Moderator band carries the right bundle branch to the anterior papillary muscle
Very sensitive to sudden afterload rises, e.g. massive pulmonary embolism
RV infarction accompanies many inferior MIs; check V4R

test.q: Which chamber of the heart is the most anterior?
test.explain: The right ventricle sits directly behind the sternum and forms most of the front surface.

test.q: The muscle band carrying the right bundle branch across the right ventricle is the ______ band.
test.explain: The moderator band (septomarginal trabecula) links the septum to the anterior papillary muscle.

test.q: The smooth outflow part of the right ventricle leading to the pulmonary valve is the:
test.explain: The infundibulum (conus arteriosus) is smooth-walled; the rest is trabeculated.

test.q: Low blood pressure, raised JVP and clear lungs after an inferior MI suggest:
test.explain: Proximal RCA occlusion can infarct the RV; confirm with right-sided lead V4R.

test.q: Echo RV free wall hypokinesis with a spared apex in pulmonary embolism is ______ sign.
test.explain: McConnell sign suggests acute RV strain, classically from pulmonary embolism.
